text: How does your database find one row among ten million so fast? With an index. It works like the index at the back of a textbook: rather than flipping through every page for a topic, you go straight to the right spot. Most indexes are built on a B-tree, which makes lookups O(log n), so doubling your data adds only one more step to the search, not twice as many. In one real case, a query on a 10M-row table dropped from 2.1 seconds to 4 milliseconds, a difference users will notice. There's a tradeoff, though. Indexes can slow writes by about 15%, because the database has to keep them up to date on every insert and update. Below, we'll look at how indexes work, when they pay off, and how to use them sensibly.
